name: Vegan diet

lead: A vegan diet excludes all animal products. In appearance circles it is used for leanness and skin, and in some anecdotal claims for lighter eye colour.

The chain is that vegan diets are higher in fibre and lower in saturated fat and shift gut microbiota, and trials of low-fat vegan diets report weight loss and better glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, which feeds into a leaner body. Skin effects are claimed rather than studied, and no trials examine looks.

paras: People build meals from legumes, grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts and soy products, and take B12 from fortified foods or supplements. Weight changes appear over weeks to months, and many pair the diet with training.

The main concern is vitamin B12, which comes only from fortified foods or supplements, plus vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron, zinc and omega-3. The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all life stages.

angle.text: People go vegan for a leaner body and clearer skin, since higher fibre and lower saturated fat can lower weight and improve cardiometabolic markers. Trials cover weight and metabolic outcomes; skin and eye-colour claims are anecdotal.

lead: A vegan diet excludes all animal-derived foods, including meat, fish, dairy, eggs and honey. The term was coined by Donald Watson and Dorothy Morgan in November 1944 when the Vegan Society was founded.[1] People in appearance communities discuss it for skin, leanness and even eye colour, though most such claims are anecdotal.

Research is mostly observational and on health outcomes. A 2017 meta-analysis examined vegetarian and vegan diets against chronic disease and mortality outcomes, randomized trials of low-fat vegan diets in type 2 diabetes reported improved glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, and a meta-analysis of randomized trials examined weight change.[2][3][4][5]

The Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets are appropriate at all life stages, while a systematic review and other literature highlight nutrients needing attention, particularly vitamin B12.[6][1]
infobox: B12, vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron, zinc, omega-3

paras: A 2017 systematic review with meta-analysis of observational studies examined vegetarian and vegan diets in relation to chronic disease risk factors, mortality, cardiovascular disease and cancer.[2] A comparison of nutritional quality found differences between vegan, vegetarian, semi-vegetarian, pesco-vegetarian and omnivorous diets.[7] A 2021 systematic review of vegan diet intake and adequacy examined which nutrients tend to fall short.[6]

Vegan diets are associated with differences in gut microbiota composition compared with omnivorous diets.[8] Modelling work has also compared vegan diets with other sustainable diets for health and environmental impact.[9] A paediatric society position paper on complementary feeding addresses infant feeding.[10] A 1991 controlled trial studied fasting followed by a vegetarian diet in rheumatoid arthritis.[11]
Wikipedia lists vitamin B12, long-chain omega-3, vitamin D, calcium, iodine, iron and zinc as nutrients of concern, and notes B12 can only come from fortified foods or supplements.[1]

Two randomized trials in type 2 diabetes compared a low-fat vegan diet with conventional diets and reported improvements in glycemic control and cardiovascular risk factors; a 2016 meta-analysis of randomized trials examined vegetarian diets and weight reduction.[3][4][5] No clinical studies were found testing vegan diets for skin quality or facial appearance.

Appearance forum threads discuss vegan diets for skin, leanness and eye colour, and others link them to bodybuilding and hair concerns.[12][13][14] Posters disagree, and the claims are mostly personal reports.

lore.intro: Vegan diets are discussed for skin, lean physique and even eye colour, with disagreement among posters.[12][14]
